## Sampling Distribtion -- Recap

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](bootstrap_vs_sampling_left.png){fig-alt="Left panel only: Sampling Distribution flowchart. A navy ellipse labelled Population with true slope beta-1 equals 2.50 at top. Three arrows lead to orange-bordered sample boxes. Green dots converge into a green bell-curve histogram labelled Sampling Distribution of beta-hat-1 with SE bracket." width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

* [Core ideas:]{.hl1}

  * The distribution of $\widehat{\beta}_{1}$ in repeated samples.

  * Useful in understanding the statistical uncertainty in $\widehat{\beta}_{1}$.

  * But also a hypothetical construct, not accessible in practice.


* [Analytical approach to a workaround:]{.hl1}

  * Make theoretical model assumptions and derive an explicit expression for ${\text{SE}}(\widehat{\beta}_{1})$ for fixed $x$.
  
  * Use this to obtain $\widehat{\text{SE}}(\widehat{\beta}_{1})$ from the (only) observed sample.
  
  * Also use them to construct confidence intervals for $\beta_{1}$.  
  
  * Generalizable to other regression parameters in multiple regression problems.
  
  * But some practical challenges still remain.
  
    * Not easily generalizable to random $x$. 
    
    * $\widehat{\text{SE}}(\widehat{\beta}_{1})$ has its own sampling fluctuations.
  
    * Not robust to model assumption violations.

:::

:::::

## Computational Solution -- Bootstrap

:::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.callout-note icon=false appearance="simple" style="display:table; border-left: 0px solid #1a2744; padding: 0px 0 0px 0px; margin: 8px auto;"}
* Start with the original sample of size $n$.

* Repeat the following process a large number $B$ times (typically $B \ge 1000$):

    -   **Step 1:** Draw a [bootstrap sample]{.hl1} by resampling $n$ times from the original sample with replacement at random.
    -   **Step 2:** Fit the regression on this bootstrap sample and record the slope $\widehat\beta_1^*$.

* Examine the [bootstrap distribution]{.hl1} of all $B$ collected $\widehat\beta_1^*$ values.

:::

* The bootstrap distribution mimics both the shape and the spread of the true sampling distribution. 

* However, it gets shifted over to center around the original sample estimate $\widehat{\beta}_{1}$. 

* This implies, while we can not use it to estimate $\beta_{1}$, we can use it to estimate the standard error: 

::: {.callout-note icon=false appearance="simple" style="display:table; border-left: 0px solid #1a2744; padding: 0px 0 0px 0px; margin: 8px auto;"}
$$\text{SD}_{\text{boot}}(\widehat{\beta}_1^{*}) \approx \text{SE}(\widehat{\beta}_1)$$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](bootstrap_vs_sampling_right.png){fig-alt="Right panel only: Bootstrap flowchart. An orange-bordered box labelled One Observed Sample with beta-hat-1 equals 2.46 at top. Three arrows lead to purple-bordered resample boxes. Purple dots converge into a purple bell-curve histogram labelled Bootstrap Distribution of beta-hat-1-star with Bootstrap SE bracket." width="100%"}
:::
::::

## Computational Solution -- Bootstrap

:::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.callout-note icon=false appearance="simple" style="display:table; border-left: 0px solid #1a2744; padding: 0px 0 0px 0px; margin: 8px auto;"}
* Start with the original sample of size $n$.

* Repeat the following process a large number $B$ times (typically $B \ge 1000$):

    -   **Step 1:** Draw a [bootstrap sample]{.hl1} by resampling $n$ times from the original sample with replacement at random.
    -   **Step 2:** Fit the regression on this bootstrap sample and record the slope $\widehat\beta_1^*$.

* Examine the [bootstrap distribution]{.hl1} of all $B$ collected $\widehat\beta_1^*$ values.

:::

* The bootstrap distribution mimics both the shape and the spread of the true sampling distribution. 

* However, it gets shifted over to center around the original sample estimate $\widehat{\beta}_{1}$. 

* This implies, we can also use it to construct confidence intervals using approximate formulas: 

::: {.callout-note icon=false appearance="simple" style="display:table; border-left: 0px solid #1a2744; padding: 0px 0 0px 0px; margin: 8px auto;"}
$$
95\% \text{ CI for } \beta_{1}: [\widehat{\beta}_{1} \pm 2 \times \text{SD}_{\text{boot}}(\widehat{\beta}_{1})]
$$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](bootstrap_vs_sampling_right.png){fig-alt="Right panel only: Bootstrap flowchart. An orange-bordered box labelled One Observed Sample with beta-hat-1 equals 2.46 at top. Three arrows lead to purple-bordered resample boxes. Purple dots converge into a purple bell-curve histogram labelled Bootstrap Distribution of beta-hat-1-star with Bootstrap SE bracket." width="100%"}
:::
::::

## Computational Solution -- Bootstrap

:::: columns

::: {.column width="50%"}

::: {.callout-note icon=false appearance="simple" style="display:table; border-left: 0px solid #1a2744; padding: 0px 0 0px 0px; margin: 8px auto;"}
* Start with the original sample of size $n$.

* Repeat the following process a large number $B$ times (typically $B \ge 1000$):

    -   **Step 1:** Draw a [bootstrap sample]{.hl1} by resampling $n$ times from the original sample with replacement at random.
    -   **Step 2:** Fit the regression on this bootstrap sample and record the slope $\widehat\beta_1^*$.

* Examine the [bootstrap distribution]{.hl1} of all $B$ collected $\widehat\beta_1^*$ values.

:::

* The bootstrap distribution mimics both the shape and the spread of the true sampling distribution. 

* However, it gets shifted over to center around the original sample estimate $\widehat{\beta}_{1}$. 

* This implies, we can also use it to construct confidence intervals using the quantiles of the bootstrap samples $\widehat{\beta}_{1}^{*}$'s: 

::: {.callout-note icon=false appearance="simple" style="display:table; border-left: 0px solid #1a2744; padding: 0px 0 0px 0px; margin: 8px auto;"}
$$
95\% \text{ CI for } \beta_{1}: [\widehat{\beta}_{1,2.5\%}^{*} , \widehat{\beta}_{1,97.5\%}^{*}]
$$
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](bootstrap_vs_sampling_right.png){fig-alt="Right panel only: Bootstrap flowchart. An orange-bordered box labelled One Observed Sample with beta-hat-1 equals 2.46 at top. Three arrows lead to purple-bordered resample boxes. Purple dots converge into a purple bell-curve histogram labelled Bootstrap Distribution of beta-hat-1-star with Bootstrap SE bracket." width="100%"}
:::
::::

* [**Why the name 'bootstrap'?**]{.hl1} drawn from the expression “to pull oneself up by one's bootstraps,” which means to improve oneself or achieve success through one's own effort, without outside help.

## Residual vs. Case Bootstrap

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="49%"}

When $x$ values are [fixed]{.hl1}; resamples **residuals** ($\widehat{e}_{i}$) only.


![](residual_bootstrap.png){width=65% fig-align="center"}

:::

::: {.column width="49%"}

When $x$ values are also [random]{.hl1} (in addition to $y$); <br>resamples **rows** $(x_i, y_i)$ jointly.


![](case_bootstrap.png){width=65% fig-align="center"}

:::

::::



---

## Residual vs. Case Bootstrap -- Key Differences

| Property | Residual Bootstrap | Case Bootstrap |
|---|---|---|
| What is resampled? | Residuals $\hat{e}_i$ | Pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ |
| $x$ values in replicate | Fixed (same as original) | Random (from original) |
| Critical assumption | Errors i.i.d. <!--model correctly specified--> | $(x, y)$ pairs i.i.d. |
| Robust to model misspecification? | No | **Yes** |
| Appropriate when $x$ is fixed by design? | **Yes** | Less natural |
| Appropriate when $x$ is random? | Less natural | **Yes** |
| Typical use case | Designed experiments | Observational studies, survey data |

<!--::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**Practical note.** In simple random sampling settings both methods are asymptotically equivalent for estimating $\text{Var}(\widehat{\beta}_1)$, but they can diverge when the error distribution is heteroskedastic or the model is misspecified — situations where the case bootstrap is generally preferred.
:::-->

## Real Data Illustration: `cars`

Let's model the relationship between speed ($x$, in mph) and stopping distance ($y$, in ft) using simple linear regression: $$dist_{i} = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}speed_{i} + \epsilon_{i}$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| comment: ""
#| cache: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 8
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center

# ── 1. Load Data, Fit Model, and Print Analytical Summary ─────────────────────
data(cars)

# Fit the original OLS model
model <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)
n <- nrow(cars)
B <- 1000 # Number of bootstrap replications

# Print original analytical summary
cat("--- Original Analytical Results ---\n")
print(round(summary(model)$coefficients["speed", 1:2],3))

# ── 2. Method A: Residual Bootstrapping ───────────────────────────────────────
# (Assumes the linear relationship and homoscedasticity are correct)
fitted_vals <- fitted(model)
residuals   <- residuals(model)

beta1_boot_res <- numeric(B)

set.seed(123) # For reproducibility
for (b in 1:B) {
  # Resample the residuals with replacement
  boot_res <- sample(residuals, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  
  # Construct new synthetic Y values
  y_star <- fitted_vals + boot_res
  
  # Refit the model with synthetic Y and original X
  boot_model <- lm(y_star ~ speed, data = cars)
  beta1_boot_res[b] <- coef(boot_model)["speed"]
}

# Calculate Residual Bootstrap SE and 95% CI
se_res <- sd(beta1_boot_res)
ci_res <- quantile(beta1_boot_res, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

cat("\n--- Residual Bootstrap Results ---\n")
cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(se_res,3), "\n")
cat("95% Percentile CI: [", round(ci_res[1],3), ",", round(ci_res[2],3), "]\n")


# ── 3. Method B: Case (Pairs) Bootstrapping ──────────────────────────────────
# (Does not assume a true linear model; robust to heteroscedasticity)
beta1_boot_pairs <- numeric(B)

set.seed(123)
for (b in 1:B) {
  # Resample the entire row indices with replacement
  boot_idx <- sample(1:n, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  boot_data <- cars[boot_idx, ]
  
  # Refit the model on the paired resamples
  boot_model <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = boot_data)
  beta1_boot_pairs[b] <- coef(boot_model)["speed"]
}

# Calculate Case Bootstrap SE and 95% CI
se_pairs <- sd(beta1_boot_pairs)
ci_pairs <- quantile(beta1_boot_pairs, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))

cat("\n--- Case (Pairs) Bootstrap Results ---\n")
cat("Bootstrap SE:", round(se_pairs,3), "\n")
cat("95% Percentile CI: [", round(ci_pairs[1],3), ",", round(ci_pairs[2],3), "]\n")

```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| comment: ""
#| cache: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 8
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-align: center

# ── 4. Plot original data and the two bootstrap distributions ─────────────────
layout(matrix(1:2, ncol = 2))

# Residual Bootstrap Distribution Plot
hist(beta1_boot_res, col = "lightblue", border = "white",
     main = "Residual Bootstrap", xlab = expression(hat(beta)[1]^"*"))
abline(v = coef(model)["speed"], col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2) # Original estimate
abline(v = ci_res, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 3) # Confidence Interval

# Case Bootstrap Distribution Plot
hist(beta1_boot_pairs, col = "lavender", border = "white",
     main = "Case Bootstrap", xlab = expression(hat(beta)[1]^"*"))
abline(v = coef(model)["speed"], col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2) # Original estimate
abline(v = ci_pairs, col = "blue", lwd = 2, lty = 3) # Confidence Interval

```
:::
::::



<!--## Key Takeaways

- The **sampling distribution** describes how $\widehat{\beta}_1$ would vary across repeated samples, but it is a theoretical construct that is typically unobservable in practice. 

- **Bootstrap** provides a computational approximation to the sampling distribution by repeatedly resampling the observed data with replacement and refitting the model. 

- The variability of the bootstrap estimates,
  $\text{SD}_{\text{boot}}(\widehat{\beta}_1^*),$
  provides an estimate of the standard error of $\widehat{\beta}_1$. 
  
- Bootstrap distributions typically reproduce the **shape and spread** of the sampling distribution, while being centered around the observed estimate $\widehat{\beta}_1$. 

- Confidence intervals can be obtained using either:
  - Approximation formulas based on the bootstrap standard error, or
  - Percentile intervals based directly on bootstrap quantiles. 

- **Residual bootstrap** is appropriate when predictor values are treated as fixed; **case bootstrap** is preferred when observations $(x_i,y_i)$ are viewed as random draws from a population. 

- Case bootstrap is generally more robust to model misspecification, whereas residual bootstrap relies more heavily on regression model assumptions. 

- **Main message:** Bootstrap methods allow us to quantify uncertainty in regression estimates using only the observed data and modern computation.
-->
